The central question is: when you slice a long document into chunks for dense retrieval, where you cut determines both how fast a query can find a relevant passage and how complete/accurate that passage is when it arrives — and these two objectives pull in opposite directions. Key concepts include chunk granularity (sentence vs. fixed-token vs. semantic boundary), the embedding collapse problem (coarse chunks average away discriminative signal, making cosine similarity less separable), passage faithfulness (whether the retrieved span actually contains a self-contained, non-truncated answer), and ANN index behavior (finer chunks mean larger corpora, which inflates both index size and approximate search error). A beginner assumes smaller chunks are strictly better because they're more "precise," not realizing that sub-sentence fragments destroy coreference chains and discourse structure, causing the LLM reader to hallucinate bridging context that was physically cut away. The expert worry is subtler: the tradeoff curve isn't monotone — there's a chunk size regime (often around 128–256 tokens with 20–30% overlap) where latency and faithfulness both degrade simultaneously, because overlap inflates the corpus without preserving the semantic boundaries that make embeddings discriminative, so you pay the retrieval cost of fine granularity without gaining the coherence of coarse granularity.

The specific failure mode is mid-entity boundary truncation: a fixed-token cutter will bisect named entities, multi-sentence reasoning chains, or tabular rows at arbitrary token positions, producing a chunk that embeds a semantically incomplete thought — the embedding then represents a "ghost concept" that has no clean query analog, inflating false-negative retrieval rates on entity-centric queries. Nakano et al.'s WebGPT work and the FiD (Fusion-in-Decoder) retrieval experiments both show that passage coherence — not just topical overlap — drives reader accuracy, and truncated entities are a primary driver of reader hallucination even when retrieval rank is correct. A semantic boundary strategy (e.g., spaCy sentence segmentation, or the paragraph-boundary detection in LlamaIndex's SentenceSplitter) prevents this by ensuring each chunk terminates at a grammatically and semantically closed unit, so the embedding captures a complete proposition rather than a fragment. To measure this offline, construct a boundary-sensitivity evaluation set: take 500+ long documents, manually annotate "critical boundary spans" (sentences containing the answer plus one bridging sentence), then measure chunk-answer containment rate (what fraction of gold answer spans fall entirely within a single retrieved chunk) across fixed-token vs. semantic strategies at identical 256-token budgets — Jaccard overlap of chunk boundaries with gold spans is a clean scalar metric. A concrete number to target: in the BEIR benchmark's TREC-COVID and NFCorpus subsets, semantic chunking recovers ~6–9% more fully-contained answer spans at rank-1 compared to fixed-token at equivalent chunk sizes, without changing the embedding model. The expert trap here is confusing retrieval recall (did the right document appear?) with span containment (was the answer span intact within the chunk?) — standard NDCG scores hide the second failure entirely.

The least-bad heuristic is split at the latest sentence boundary before the token limit, then carry the first sentence of the split chunk as a prefix into the next chunk — this is the "sentence-window" strategy implemented in LlamaIndex's SentenceWindowNodeParser and echoed in Anthropic's contextual retrieval writeup, where a small surrounding context is prepended to each chunk before embedding. This is strictly better than mid-sentence truncation because it preserves the embedding's propositional integrity on both sides of the cut, at the cost of ~5–8% token redundancy — acceptable given that the alternative is one chunk with a dangling clause whose embedding drifts toward the wrong query neighborhood. The choice of heuristic is diagnostic: if switching from hard-truncation to sentence-carry-forward measurably improves your end-to-end answer quality, your bottleneck is the reader, because the retriever was already surfacing the right document neighborhood but the reader was failing to reconstruct bridged arguments from incomplete spans. Conversely, if the improvement shows up in retrieval recall (MRR, NDCG@10) rather than in reader accuracy (exact match, ROUGE-L), the bottleneck is the retriever — the embedding of a truncated 480-token paragraph was collapsing discriminative signal, and the cleaner split produces a more queryable vector. The Ma et al. 2023 "Fine-Grained Late Interaction" work is instructive here: they found that for technical documents (legal, biomedical), paragraph-length chunks hurt retrieval precision more than reader coherence, implying the retriever is the binding constraint in dense-text domains. A practical diagnostic is to run retrieval in oracle mode — feed the reader the gold chunk directly — and measure the gap between oracle reader accuracy and pipeline accuracy; if that gap is large, fix the reader context first, and the 480-token conflict is a reader problem, not a retriever problem.

If oracle retrieval still fails, the embedding geometry is exonerated — by definition you handed the reader the correct chunk — so the failure implicates either reader context misallocation (the model attends to the wrong sub-span within the 480-token window) or missing inter-chunk bridging facts that the multi-hop chain requires but that live in a different chunk entirely. The "lost in the middle" finding from Liu et al. 2023 is directly relevant: transformer readers systematically underweight content positioned in the middle of long contexts, so a 480-token paragraph containing a bridging inference at token 240 will be misread even when fully present, because attention sinks pull probability mass toward the opening and closing tokens. To isolate context misallocation from missing-fact failure, run a surgical ablation: construct a minimal synthetic chunk containing only the two or three sentences strictly necessary for the hop, strip all surrounding prose, and re-query the reader — if accuracy jumps substantially (empirically, 15–25% on HotpotQA-style multi-hop sets), the problem is attention dilution over long context, not missing facts. If accuracy stays flat on the stripped chunk, the reader genuinely lacks a bridging fact, which means your chunking strategy is severing a necessary reasoning edge — the fix is graph-aware chunking or explicit entity-linking across chunk boundaries, as implemented in Microsoft's GraphRAG. The embedding geometry angle is still worth probing separately: run a nearest-neighbor audit on the query embedding against all chunk embeddings in the multi-hop chain and check whether all necessary hops appear in top-20 retrieval — if hop-2 chunks score below rank 50, the embedding space isn't preserving the inferential path, a failure that oracle experiments mask entirely. Concretely, Trivedi et al.'s IRCoT (2023) showed that interleaving retrieval with chain-of-thought generation recovers ~8–12 F1 points on MuSiQue precisely because single-shot retrieval cannot represent the conditional dependency between hops in a static embedding.

Iterative retrieval demotes chunking strategy to a secondary concern precisely when each hop's bridging fact is a self-contained, independently queryable proposition — meaning the intermediate reasoning step generates a query string that is semantically close to a chunk that exists intact somewhere in the index, regardless of how boundaries were drawn. In this regime, chunking sloppiness is absorbed by the iteration: even if hop-1 returns a truncated chunk, the reader extracts enough signal to formulate a hop-2 query that lands on the correct neighborhood, and the chain converges. Chunking remains the binding constraint even under iteration when the bridging fact is syntactically embedded inside a larger argumentative unit and cannot be queried in isolation — for example, a causal clause inside a 480-token methods paragraph where the critical dependency ("X was measured after Y was controlled") has no standalone query representation; no iterative step will generate an embedding that retrieves that clause if it was severed from its governing sentence. The Trivedi et al. IRCoT results support this directly: IRCoT's gains are concentrated on 2-hop questions (+12 F1 on MuSiQue) but diminish on questions requiring numerical or causal reasoning embedded in dense prose, precisely because iteration cannot manufacture a query for a fact that has no clean propositional surface form. A second condition where chunking stays binding is corpus scale: at 10M+ chunks, each iterative retrieval call adds 50–200ms latency, so systems like Bing's RAG infrastructure cap iteration depth at 2–3 hops, meaning any reasoning chain longer than the iteration budget forces all remaining hops back onto single-shot retrieval quality — and chunk boundary quality directly determines whether those hops succeed. The clean diagnostic is to measure hop-query coherence: for each generated intermediate query in an IRCoT trace, compute its maximum cosine similarity to any chunk in the index; if that ceiling similarity is below ~0.75 (on normalized embeddings with a model like E5-large), the fact is unchunkable-as-queried and iteration cannot rescue it regardless of depth.

response:
The highest-leverage indexing-time intervention is proposition indexing: decompose each chunk into atomic propositions using an LLM at index time, embed each proposition independently, but store a pointer back to the parent chunk so the reader receives full context on retrieval — this is the architecture from Chen et al.'s "Dense X Retrieval" (2023), which showed 10–15% improvement in hit rate on ODQA benchmarks precisely because each embedded unit now has a clean propositional surface form that iterative queries can match. For causal chains specifically, you augment this with explicit relation extraction: run an IE pass (spaCy's dependency parser or a fine-tuned REBEL model) to surface causal and conditional triples (X→Y, "controlled before measured"), embed those triples as synthetic documents alongside the propositions, and index them under a separate HNSW partition — this gives iterative retrieval a direct handle on the relational structure that prose embedding collapses. For numerical reasoning, the equivalent intervention is table and formula canonicalization: extract numerical claims into structured templates ("metric X = value Y in condition Z"), embed the template string rather than the surrounding prose, and link back to source — this is what Microsoft's NLM-Num and the TAT-QA system do to avoid numerical facts drowning in narrative context. The indexing cost is severe and three-dimensional: proposition extraction via LLM adds roughly 5–10x the embedding compute of naive chunking (you're running a generation pass over every chunk, not just an encoder forward pass), corpus size expands 3–6x inflating ANN index memory and build time, and maintaining parent-chunk pointers requires a secondary document store (typically a key-value layer like Redis or a metadata column in Weaviate/Qdrant). The quality-cost tradeoff is non-uniform across document types: for technical and scientific corpora where causal density is high, proposition indexing recovers enough hop-query coherence to justify the cost; for narrative or conversational documents, the propositions are often so simple that vanilla semantic chunking already achieves near-ceiling coherence, making the overhead unjustifiable. The practical decision rule is to measure propositional density (average number of extractable atomic claims per 256-token chunk) on a sample of your corpus before committing — if it exceeds ~4 propositions per chunk, the collision in embedding space is severe enough that proposition indexing will pay for itself.

Flat HNSW becomes architecturally untenable at roughly 50–100M vectors at 768 dimensions, where the in-memory footprint hits 150–300GB and build time exceeds 12–24 hours on a single high-memory node — with proposition indexing's 3–6x expansion, this threshold is crossed at a source corpus of only 10–30M original chunks, which is well within the range of enterprise document collections or mid-scale web retrieval. The first forced transition is to IVF-PQ (inverted file with product quantization, the backbone of Faiss's IVF_HNSW and Weaviate's PQ compression): PQ compresses each 768-dim vector to 64–128 bytes by encoding sub-vector clusters, reducing memory 6–12x, but the quantization error introduces a recall penalty of 3–8% at R@10 compared to exact HNSW — concretely, if your flat index achieved 87% R@10, PQ compression typically floors you at 80–84%, and that gap maps directly onto downstream answer quality for the hardest multi-hop queries where rank-10 is the marginal retrieval. At 500M–1B+ vectors (large-scale proposition indexes over web corpora), IVF-PQ itself becomes unwieldy and the shift moves to learned indexes or hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval: ScaNN (Google, 2020) uses anisotropic quantization to better preserve inner-product geometry, recovering ~2–3% recall over vanilla PQ at equivalent memory, while DiskANN pushes the graph index to NVMe SSD with a DRAM cache layer, tolerating 3–5x latency increase in exchange for holding only the top graph layers in memory. The quality surrender in the tiered transition is asymmetric: high-similarity retrievals degrade minimally because quantization error is small relative to the large inner-product gap, but hard negatives — vectors at cosine similarity 0.72–0.78 from the query — get reranked incorrectly at much higher rates, and these are precisely the proposition vectors for semantically adjacent but causally distinct claims that multi-hop reasoning depends on. Facebook's 2021 analysis of IVF-PQ on BEIR showed that biomedical and technical subsets (NFCorpus, TREC-COVID) suffer disproportionately in the transition because their embedding distributions are tighter and more isotropic than general-domain text, meaning PQ cluster boundaries cut through semantically meaningful neighborhoods rather than between them. The practical mitigation is a two-stage pipeline: use the compressed index for candidate generation (top-100 with PQ) then re-rank with exact inner products over the full-precision vectors of only those 100 candidates — this recovers 90–95% of flat HNSW quality at a fraction of the memory cost, and is the architecture Qdrant, Vespa, and Pinecone all converge on at scale.

Yes, this conflict is real and empirically documented: hard-negative training explicitly pulls semantically similar but distinct propositions apart in embedding space, which concentrates the learned representation in a tighter, more anisotropic manifold — and anisotropic distributions are precisely what break PQ's assumption that sub-vector dimensions are approximately independent and uniformly distributed across cluster centroids. The evidence comes from Matryoshka Representation Learning (Kusupati et al., 2022) and the isotropy analysis in Ethayarajh (2019): both show that contrastive training with hard negatives increases the variance explained by the top principal components, meaning the embedding mass migrates toward a lower-dimensional subspace — PQ then assigns disproportionate centroid budget to that subspace while the orthogonal dimensions (which still carry residual discriminative signal for the hard-negative pairs) get coarsely quantized. Concretely, E5-large and BGE-large trained with mined hard negatives from the 0.70–0.80 similarity band show 4–7% higher R@10 on BEIR versus models trained with random negatives, but their PQ recall penalty at the same compression ratio widens from ~4% to 7–11%, effectively erasing half the retrieval quality gain when the index is compressed — this tradeoff appears in the BGE technical report's ablations though it isn't foregrounded. The mechanism is precise: hard-negative training increases the effective intrinsic dimensionality of the discriminative subspace around contested query regions, and PQ's fixed codebook size (typically 256 centroids per sub-vector) cannot allocate enough resolution to those regions without degrading coverage elsewhere. The practical escape hatches are residual quantization (RQ, used in ScaNN and the Faiss RQ index), which applies successive quantization rounds to the residual error and partially recovers the lost resolution, and OPQ (Optimized PQ), which learns a rotation matrix aligning the embedding dimensions with PQ's independence assumption before quantization — OPQ recovers roughly 2–4% of the recall penalty at no memory cost, though it adds a one-time rotation-fitting step at index build time. The deeper implication is that embedding model selection and index architecture cannot be optimized independently: a model trained to maximize retrieval quality on hard negatives should be paired with RQ or OPQ rather than vanilla PQ, and benchmarks that evaluate embedding models against exact HNSW systematically overstate their deployable quality at the corpus scales where compression is mandatory.
